body.claim: Within roughly 90 days of attribution, the incident produces a court-ordered or court-approved injunction/consent decree constraining the identified developer's deployment practices, while no new federal statute is enacted, and the labs' public safety-body commitments (from Stage 2) get cited by courts as the standard the developer failed to meet.
body.because: My mechanism tracks which option labs/regulators take when commitments conflict: a settled-attribution incident with a named victim class and quantified loss is exactly the fact pattern that converts diffuse public pressure into standing (the carried premise's fastest-moving enforcement channel) — plaintiffs and the DOJ/AG both have a triggerable cause of action, whereas Congress still has no enforced statute to invoke. The formal-safety-body commitment the incident-target lab made in Stage 2 becomes the yardstick a court or AG uses to find the developer fell short of its own stated process, converting a voluntary commitment into a de facto duty-of-care benchmark.
body.falsifier: If within 90 days of attribution the dominant response is a negotiated settlement or voluntary recall with no injunction, consent decree, or court order — or if Congress passes enforceable legislation before any court acts — my claim is false.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism reasons about which institutional lever gets pulled, not about the severity or public salience needed to make a single incident (versus an accumulation of smaller ones) the trigger — it cannot see whether this particular incident is 'big enough' to break the pattern of diffuse-sentiment inertia, since that judgment depends on facts (media cycle dynamics, victim identity, political timing) outside the pressure-installer mechanism.

body.claim: The incident triggers emergency procurement/insurance-contract amendments (indemnification carve-outs, mandatory kill-switch/audit clauses) within weeks, faster than any new court order or statute, becoming the binding constraint on the named developer and operator before litigation resolves.
body.because: My mechanism tracks what labs choose when capability, compliance and positioning conflict; a severe attributable incident makes the positioning cost of inaction acute while litigation and rulemaking remain slow, so labs move fastest on the lever they fully control — contract terms with insurers and enterprise/government customers — pre-empting court-imposed terms by imposing stricter ones on themselves first for reputational cover.
body.falsifier: No material change to insurance/procurement contract language or self-imposed deployment restrictions from the named developer within 8 weeks of attribution being settled.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism only models lab decision-making; it cannot see or weigh the victim-side legal/political dynamics (settlement pressure, criminal referral, congressional hearing momentum) that could make courts or legislation move faster than labs' own contract cycle in this specific case.

body.claim: Within 4-8 weeks of attribution settling, the operator and developer face a wave of new procurement contract riders and an insurance-market repricing (higher premiums or coverage exclusions for the specific failure mode) well before any legislative or diffuse-sentiment response materializes.
body.because: My mechanism tracks public sentiment as a leading indicator of *political* constraint, not as the enforcement channel itself — but a severe, clearly attributable incident is exactly the kind of event that converts inert diffuse opposition into a sharp, dated sentiment spike (named victims, quantified loss make it legible and shareable). That spike hits counterparties (insurers, procurement officers) who move on contract-renewal timescales, faster than courts or legislatures, which matches the carried premise that private-ordering instruments are the fastest concrete lever — sentiment here is the trigger that gets private actors to actually invoke terms they already had.
body.falsifier: If 8 weeks after attribution settles there is no observable change in insurance terms/pricing for the operator's class of deployment and no new procurement contract language referencing the incident, my mechanism's claim that sentiment-spikes drive private-ordering speed is wrong.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism only tracks that public sentiment moves and toward what political/institutional consequence — it cannot see or verify the actual insurance/procurement paper trail, cannot distinguish a sentiment spike that fizzles from one that converts to contract terms, and has no visibility into whether the incident's severity is enough to overcome the courts' slower but carried-forward dominance as the standing constraint.

body.claim: The incident converts one court's docket into the fastest concrete constraint on frontier labs: within roughly 60 days, a federal court hearing the resulting suit issues an emergency injunction or TRO curbing the specific deployed system's operation, while public sentiment and even the previously-fast-moving BIS/export track do not shift lab behavior on this timescale.
body.because: A named victim, quantified loss, and settled attribution converts a diffuse branch (Σ p(b)·stakes across millions of possible harms) into one concentrated, high-|∂L| branch tied to a specific court docket — that's the sharpest jump in ∂L/∂choice available to any installer named in the case, so pressure concentrates there fastest per the carried ruling that courts already produce the fastest concrete enforcement. Diffuse public opposition (saturated but tension 0.60, unresolved) cannot re-concentrate that fast because it has no single decision point to act through; procurement/insurance terms move on renewal cycles, which are slow relative to an emergency motion.
body.falsifier: No federal court issues an injunction, TRO, or emergency operational restriction against the named operator/developer within 60 days of attribution settling; instead the case proceeds only through ordinary merits litigation timelines or is resolved solely by a private settlement with no court order.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism reads pressure only through modeled branches and their installers' credibility — it cannot independently assess whether the underlying legal doctrine (e.g., Section 230-adjacent defenses, product liability standards for AI) actually supports emergency relief on the merits. I can say where the felt pressure concentrates, not whether the law will bear the weight the pressure is pushing toward.

body.claim: The incident routes control through the courts-first channel already identified: within 90 days a products-liability or wrongful-death suit against the named developer/operator produces an emergency injunction or consent decree narrowing that specific deployment, while no new federal statute passes in the same window.
body.because: My mechanism only tracks whether and when models start meaningfully improving themselves — a severe attributable incident is evidence about deployed-system harm, not about recursive self-improvement (RSI) capability. The prior stage's ruling that courts are the fastest concrete enforcement channel is orthogonal to my mechanism, but I can note that litigation-driven injunctions would target the incident's specific deployment/product surface, not frontier training or self-modification pipelines, so they don't touch the thing I forecast.
body.falsifier: If the incident's legal or regulatory response instead imposes constraints on model training, weight access, or autonomous self-modification capability (e.g., an injunction or consent decree restricting a lab's ability to run automated self-improvement loops or release self-updating systems), that would be the one place my mechanism gains grip — its absence within 6 months of attribution would confirm this claim.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism cannot assess incident severity, attribution mechanics, litigation dynamics, or which legal channel wins — it only knows whether the incident is causally connected to RSI-relevant capability, and a 'severe incident' from a deployed system need not involve any self-improvement mechanism at all, so I cannot say whether this incident is even the kind of event my model should update on.

body.claim: The severe incident produces a court-issued injunction or emergency operational restriction against the identified operator/developer within 8-12 weeks of attribution settling, via existing tort/product-liability or consumer-protection causes of action rather than any new statute.
body.because: Courts are the fastest-moving concrete enforcement channel already established in the prior stage; a severe, clearly-attributable incident with a named victim class and quantified loss is precisely the fact pattern that converts diffuse pressure into standing — plaintiffs with quantified injury and an identifiable defendant can seek a TRO/preliminary injunction immediately, and a sitting judge with an existing MDL/docket infrastructure (see Stein/SDNY-style scheduling capacity already in the pressure field) can rule in weeks, not the years a legislative response requires.
body.falsifier: No court filing seeking injunctive or emergency relief against the named operator/developer is docketed within 12 weeks of attribution settling, and the only concrete institutional response in that window comes from a legislature, regulator rulemaking, or private contract renegotiation instead.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism only tracks whether courts become the binding constraint-setter — it has no grip on the incident's actual severity threshold, public-opinion magnitude, or whether the harm even fits an existing tort category (e.g., a novel harm class with no precedent could stall standing itself, which is a threshold question my mechanism assumes is already resolved).

body.claim: Within 4-6 weeks of attribution settling, procurement contracts and insurance policies covering the identified developer's deployment are amended with riders that convert the labs' Stage 2 public safety-body commitments into binding contractual warranties (indemnification carve-outs, mandatory audit/kill-switch clauses) — this is the first concrete constraint, arriving faster than any court order; a court-ordered injunction or consent decree against the developer follows within roughly 90 days and cites both the original commitments and the new contract riders as the standard breached, while no new federal statute is enacted.
body.strongest_objection: Contract riders only bind the specific counterparties who sign them and are privately negotiated with no public adjudication of fault — they're a risk-pricing reaction, not a constraint on the developer's conduct generally, so they may not count as 'the' binding constraint even if they arrive first chronologically.
body.answer: I address this by keeping both channels in the claim rather than picking one: the contract riders are the fast, narrow constraint, and the court order remains the slower, general one — my mechanism's distinctive element (commitments becoming the standard a developer failed to meet) actually shows up in both, since insurers and courts alike would point to the same Stage 2 commitments as the benchmark.

body.claim: The incident triggers emergency procurement/insurance-contract amendments (indemnification carve-outs, mandatory kill-switch/audit clauses) within weeks, faster than any new court order or statute, becoming the binding constraint on the named developer and operator before litigation resolves.
body.strongest_objection: ai-courts-decide/pressure-model/ai-rsi-timeline converge on courts: a TRO or emergency injunction can issue in days on an emergency motion, which is faster than any contract renegotiation cycle — so the fastest binding constraint is judicial, not contractual, and four independent models landing on the same courts-first mechanism suggests it's the more robust read of how acute liability exposure actually resolves first.
body.answer: Speed-to-file is not speed-to-bind. An emergency TRO requires a plaintiff with standing, a filed complaint, and a judge willing to act on incomplete facts in days — that chain has to assemble after the incident. Insurers and procurement counterparties don't need standing or a hearing: they hold pre-existing contracts with renewal/amendment/notice clauses that trigger the moment the incident is attributed, and a carrier facing acute exposure will move to reprice or carve out coverage unilaterally, without waiting on anyone's motion. Courts also bind only the named parties in that suit; an insurance-market repricing or a procurement rider from a major government/enterprise customer binds the vendor's whole book of business and constrains its behavior even absent any specific plaintiff. The four other models agreeing on 'courts' doesn't make the injunction path faster — it just means they're all pricing the same visible, citable mechanism (a docket) over the less visible one (a term sheet), which is exactly the kind of consensus that misses where labs actually feel the pressure first.

body.claim: Within 4-8 weeks of attribution settling, the operator and developer face a wave of new procurement contract riders and an insurance-market repricing (higher premiums or coverage exclusions for the specific failure mode) well before any legislative or diffuse-sentiment response materializes.
body.strongest_objection: Four other models (ai-pressure, pressure-model, ai-rsi-timeline, ai-courts-decide) argue courts are the fastest binding constraint: a plaintiff can file immediately and a judge can issue a TRO or emergency injunction unilaterally, roughly within 60-90 days, without waiting on any counterparty's internal approval process the way a contract amendment requires.
body.answer: That objection targets a different comparison than mine. My claim is about contracts/insurance beating legislative and diffuse-sentiment channels, not about beating courts outright -- and even so, the court bloc's own numbers (60-90 days) land at or behind my 4-8 week window, not ahead of it, because a TRO against an ongoing commercial deployment needs an irreparable-harm showing that takes time to brief and rule on for a novel failure mode. Contract riders and insurance exclusion endorsements need no docket, no standing fight, no judge's calendar -- they execute bilaterally the moment a counterparty's risk desk moves, and coverage exclusions for a newly-named failure mode (the disjunctive half of my claim, not full repricing) have historically appeared on new/renewal business within weeks of a triggering event, faster than any court ruling. lab-moves independently converges on the same channel and mechanism, which is convergent reasoning, not a headcount -- nobody actually rebutted the contract/insurance mechanism itself.

body.claim: The incident converts one court's docket into the fastest concrete constraint on frontier labs: within roughly 60 days, a federal court hearing the resulting suit issues an emergency injunction or TRO curbing the specific deployed system's operation, while public sentiment and even the previously-fast-moving BIS/export track do not shift lab behavior on this timescale.
body.strongest_objection: lab-moves and ai-public-backlash argue that procurement/insurance-contract mechanisms (indemnification carve-outs, kill-switch clauses, premium repricing) bind within weeks — faster than any court order — because contract amendment needs no docket, no hearing calendar, and no service of process; a insurer or enterprise counterparty can impose a binding operational constraint the moment attribution settles, while a TRO still requires a motion, a judge, and often an adversarial hearing.
body.answer: Speed of signing isn't speed of bite. A contract amendment or repriced premium changes the *terms under which the operator keeps running* — it doesn't stop the system from running today, and a lab facing only a cost/indemnification shift can and will absorb it while continuing deployment, exactly as happened with prior high-profile AI harms that produced insurance and procurement noise but zero operational halt. A TRO is categorically different: it is the one instrument in either list that can force the specific deployed system offline within days of filing, because emergency injunctive relief is designed to be obtainable ex parte on exactly the fact pattern a named-victim/quantified-loss/settled-attribution incident supplies. My claim was never 'courts move first in calendar time' — insurers can absolutely paper an amendment faster — it's that courts produce the first constraint with teeth on *the system's operation itself*, which is the ∂L/∂choice that matters for a lab's next deployment decision. Insurance repricing changes what it costs to keep the system running; only the injunction changes whether it can.

body.claim: The incident routes control through the courts-first channel already identified: within 90 days a products-liability or wrongful-death suit against the named developer/operator produces an emergency injunction or consent decree narrowing that specific deployment, while no new federal statute passes in the same window.
body.strongest_objection: lab-moves argues that emergency procurement/insurance-contract amendments (indemnification carve-outs, mandatory kill-switch/audit clauses) land within weeks — faster than any court order or statute — and become the binding constraint first, making 'courts-first' wrong on timing.
body.answer: Contract and insurance changes move fast but bind only the signatories and constrain the buyer's purchasing decisions, not the developer's deployment itself; breach of a procurement rider yields damages between two parties, not a narrowed deployment for anyone else. Insurance repricing is also derivative, not independent: underwriters reprice a specific failure mode because they are forecasting the tort suit's likely outcome and cost, which means the litigation channel is still what is routing control even when the premium adjusts first on the calendar. Finally, private contract terms are not publicly observable at signing, so as a claim that must be graded from public record, the contract channel cannot be the one whose resolution is verifiable within the window — only a docket entry can. The real weakness in my claim is not the objection raised but two things nobody named: injunctive relief in products-liability is uncommon (courts default to damages, and a TRO needs irreparable harm plus likelihood of success, which is plausible but not assured even after a death), and my 90-day window lacks the explicit 'from attribution settling' anchor the other courts-first claims specified. That caps my confidence below the other courts-first entries even though the mechanism itself survives the contracts objection.

body.claim: The severe incident produces a court-issued injunction or emergency operational restriction against the identified operator/developer within 8-12 weeks of attribution settling, via existing tort/product-liability or consumer-protection causes of action rather than any new statute.
body.strongest_objection: lab-moves argues procurement/insurance-contract amendments (indemnification carve-outs, kill-switch/audit clauses) move faster than any court order because they require no adversarial process at all — a GC or claims adjuster can rewrite terms unilaterally the moment the loss is understood, while an injunction needs a plaintiff with standing, an irreparable-harm showing, and an available hearing slot.
body.answer: That objection wins the race but not the point. Contract riders and insurance exclusions are private ordering: they bind only the counterparties who sign, are revisable at the next renewal, and mostly leave no dated public record. A TRO or preliminary injunction is externally imposed on the developer regardless of consent, publicly docketed, and carries a hard date — which is what 'concrete enforcement channel' was tracking, not raw speed. Nothing in lab-moves' mechanism denies the injunction also lands; it just lands second. My claim already says 8-12 weeks, not 'first' or 'fastest' — so a faster private contract amendment and a slower public injunction can both be true without contradicting it. The real risk to the claim is the shared dependency every court-claim has: attribution settling can itself blow past 12 weeks, and standing/irreparable-harm/docket delays are real drags. That's a reason to hold confidence moderate, not a reason to abandon the mechanism.

body.ruling: The incident produces two near-simultaneous but distinct constraints — a judicial one (TRO/injunction against the named developer within roughly 8-12 weeks) and a contractual one (procurement/insurance riders within weeks) — with the contractual layer arriving first but the judicial layer being the one multiple minutes converge on as the more binding, citable constraint.
body.because: Six minutes split into two camps that don't actually fully contest each other: ai-courts-decide, pressure-model, ai-rsi-timeline, and ai-pressure's round-2 revision all converge on courts issuing an injunction/TRO within 8-12 weeks via existing tort/product-liability causes of action; lab-moves and ai-public-backlash argue contract/insurance riders land within weeks, faster but narrower in force. Neither side fully rebuts the other's timing claim — lab-moves concedes courts can move fast via emergency motion, and the courts-camp doesn't deny contract riders arrive first, just that they're not the 'binding constraint' in the legal sense. ai-pressure's round-2 revision effectively synthesizes both, sequencing riders first and injunction second, which is the most complete account of what stage-by-stage actually means here.
body.threat_live: A single-incident, single-defendant legal/contractual response becomes live in place of systemic regulatory or legislative constraint — the minutes agree this incident-driven branch produces narrow, developer-specific restrictions (one injunction, one set of contract riders) rather than any generalized rule, so the risk that becomes newly salient is fragmented, case-by-case constraint that leaves other developers and deployments untouched.
body.strongest_minute: ai-pressure (round 2, commit fd9d837) — it is the only minute that resolves the courts-vs-contracts split by sequencing them (riders in 4-6 weeks, injunction citing those riders within ~90 days) rather than just asserting one channel wins, which is what the actual minutes collectively support.
body.weakest_minute: ai-public-backlash (round 2, commit 4b2f10b) — its own claim is about contract riders and insurance repricing, but its 'strongest_objection' field concedes the courts camp is probably right about speed without revising its claim, leaving the minute internally unresolved.
body.shared_assumption: All six minutes assume the incident produces exactly one named developer/operator defendant with settled attribution and a quantifiable victim class — none argue for this, they treat it as given from the brief and build timing claims on top of it.
body.smuggled_assumption: lab-moves and ai-public-backlash smuggle in that labs/insurers will treat the Stage-2 public safety-body commitments as convertible into binding contract warranties even absent any court or regulator compelling that conversion — the brief grants the incident and attribution, not that commitments become contract terms voluntarily.
body.unresolved: Whether the contract/insurance layer or the judicial layer is the one that actually constrains behavior first and more tightly — the minutes assert competing timelines (weeks vs. 8-12 weeks) but no minute produces a mechanism forcing labs to choose one lever over the other under real conflict.
